title: The Great Reversal: Gregg Williams by Two as David Mullin Takes the Spoon

articles.headline: Gregg Williams Turns Spoon Into Trophy
articles.standfirst: Holder of the Wooden Spoon going into TEG 5, Williams seized the Trophy lead at the 3rd hole of Round 3 and held it through a ruinous stretch at Palmares to win by two.
paragraphs: Gregg Williams won the TEG 5 Trophy at Lagos, six under net par and two clear of Jon Baker. He arrived holding the Wooden Spoon. He left holding the Trophy. The distance between those two objects is shorter than anyone in this field would care to admit. It ranks third among Williams's own Trophy returns, a detail he is under no obligation to raise again.

For much of the tournament it belonged to someone else. David Mullin took the net lead late on the opening day at Boavista and held it from the 18th hole of Round 1 across 21 holes, which is precisely long enough to become attached to something. Williams passed him at the 3rd in Round 3: a par on the par five, worth two under net. No thunderclap. A five, and the leaderboard quietly rearranged itself.

The damage had been done the day before. Williams's Round 2 at Boavista, 27 over gross for six under net, was the best round of his career by that measure, and it came on his ninth visit to the course, eight strokes better than his previous appearance there. It also erased a Round 1 in which he had contrived a nine at the 17th.
Baker's own chance went at Boavista in Round 3, where he made two quintuple-bogey nines, at the 7th and again at the closing hole. One is misfortune. Two is a theme.

That left Williams with room to survive Palmares, a first visit for the group, and he used every inch of it. He dropped ten shots across holes 10 to 13, then added another nine at the 16th, the whole sequence conducted with the calm of a man who had checked the arithmetic and found he could afford it. It was enough. Mullin took the TEG 5 Green Jacket on gross.

articles.headline: Record Six Birdies, One Wooden Spoon
articles.standfirst: David Mullin arrived as defending champion, led the Trophy by five at the 1st in Round 3 and set an all-time TEG birdie record at Palmares — then finished last, two behind Henry Meller.
paragraphs: David Mullin led the TEG 5 Trophy on net-versus-par from the 18th hole of the opening round, and held it for 21 holes across three rounds. He set a course best at Boavista along the way: his 82 in Round 2 beat the 85 that had stood as his best there through seven previous visits. He was leading the Trophy, walking towards the Green Jacket and holding a course record. There was nowhere left to go but down, and he went with commitment.

The lead went at the third hole of Round 3, a par five he played in five for a net two. Not a mistake. Simply not enough, as Gregg Williams moved ahead. Round 3 then became Mullin's worst round to date, +12 net and +27 gross, including a nine at the 13th, a par five, for a quadruple bogey.

At Palmares, a course none of the field had played before, he took another nine at the par-five 6th. That one hole dropped him from fourth to last in the TEG 5 Wooden Spoon race, and he stayed there, unbothered and unassisted. He finished the Trophy fifth, having been first after Round 1, and collected the Spoon at +12 net.

The oddity is that the same four rounds produced his best scoring, too. Back-to-back birdies at the 12th and 13th in Round 4 tied the all-time TEG record for consecutive birdies, and his six birdies or better across TEG 5 is an all-time TEG record for a single tournament. The Spoon and the record belong to the same four rounds, and largely to the same afternoon at Palmares.

articles.headline: History's Lowest Round, Then A Nine
articles.standfirst: Stuart Neumann's -9 at Boavista in Round 2 is the lowest round TEG has recorded; twenty-four hours later he dropped ten shots over the same three closing holes.
paragraphs: On the Monday at Boavista, Stuart Neumann played the best round in TEG history. His -9 net was a record, and his +11 gross was a record too: an 82 on a course he had already visited seven times, where his previous best was 89. Twelve strokes better than his last visit there, and a course personal best by a distance. For one afternoon he was, incontestably, the finest golfer the tournament had ever produced.

The Tuesday at the same course took it all back. He opened proceedings with a 7 at the par-three 2nd, a quadruple bogey, which turned out to be merely the overture. The round was lost over the closing stretch: a double bogey 7 at the 16th, a triple bogey 7 at the 17th and a quintuple bogey 9 at the 18th. Ten gross shots in three holes, with no net par among them.

Wednesday's move to Palmares, the first TEG visit to the course, offered a clean slate, and he declined it. Triple bogey, triple bogey, double bogey through the 2nd, 3rd and 4th: eight shots gone in three holes. He at least finished tidily, playing the 16th, 17th and 18th in level par gross, worth three net shots to par, for a round of 96 on a course nobody in the field had seen before. The man who set the record and the man who signed for the 96 were, technically, the same man.

articles.headline: Second By Two, Undone By Four Holes
articles.standfirst: Jon Baker outplayed Gregg Williams over two of the four rounds and still lost the TEG 5 Trophy by two; a pair of nines at Boavista in Round 3 is where it went.
paragraphs: Jon Baker's TEG 5 ended with the finest golf of his career and no trophy to show for it. What came before was littered with wreckage: a quintuple-bogey 8 at Boavista's par-three 6th in round one, then two nines in round three, at the par-four 7th and again at the par-four 18th to close the day. Between them came a passage of genuine competence, holes 9 to 12, worth four shots to par on net.

The final round at Palmares, a course none of the field had played before, produced more of both. Jon opened with five net shots gained across the first four holes, including a birdie at the short 3rd, then put an 8 on the par-three 5th, which is a substantial quantity of golf for a hole of that size. What followed was the moment of the tournament for him: birdies at the 14th and 15th, back to back, tying the all-time TEG record for consecutive birdies.

The round added up to a gross 90, +18, the best gross round Jon Baker has recorded. It hauled him from 19 behind in the TEG 5 Green Jacket race to 12 at the finish. It did not overhaul the TEG 5 Trophy leader. His Boavista scoring had already been eight strokes better than his last visit there; the arithmetic still declined to help.

articles.headline: Meller Escapes The Spoon By Two
articles.standfirst: Last in the field after Rounds 2 and 3, and the owner of a 10 at Boavista's 16th, Henry Meller answered with the best round of his TEG career on a course nobody had seen before.
paragraphs: Henry Meller's rounds at Boavista gave little warning of how it would end. His second round produced three of the tournament's biggest holes: a 10 at the par-five 16th, the worst score against par he has recorded anywhere; an 8 at the par-four 18th; and a 7 at the par-three 14th. The round finished 30 over gross, with a twelve-shot split between his two nines, one of which was plainly having a different day from the other.

Round three was steadier without ever threatening much. Pars at the 3rd, 4th and 5th, then a double bogey at the short 6th. His 91 was the best of his three visits to Boavista in this tournament, four strokes better than his last round there, though still short of the 89 he shot on the course in TEG 3.

Palmares, played for the first time in round four, changed the picture. The damage arrived early and got itself over with: seven shots dropped across holes 9 to 11, a triple bogey at the 9th followed by doubles at the 10th and 11th. Everything else held. Meller signed for 89, three under his handicap allowance and a personal best both on net and on gross, where +17 bettered anything he had managed in four TEGs. A man with two Wooden Spoons, bottom of the race after Rounds 2 and 3, had chosen the final available day to play the best golf of his life.
It was enough to close the gap in the TEG 5 Green Jacket from a peak of 30 shots to 18 by the finish.

articles.headline: Mullin Wins Fourth Jacket With Record 82
articles.standfirst: The gross title was over by Monday evening: David Mullin's 82 at Boavista beat a course record that had survived 35 prior TEG visits, and the two rounds he then played from the bottom half of the field could not undo it.
paragraphs: David Mullin won the TEG 5 Green Jacket at +72 gross, 12 clear of Jon Baker, and the contest was effectively decided over the first two days at Boavista.

He opened with a gross round of +12, the lowest gross round recorded in TEG to that point. He then bettered it the following day with +11, a gross 82 that set a new Boavista course record and swept aside the 85 that had stood across 35 prior visits to the Howard Swan parkland at Lagos. The 85 had been Mullin's own mark, set at TEG 3 on one of his seven previous visits. He therefore spent the afternoon dismantling himself, nine strokes better than his last time round the course. The same round was a personal best against the Trophy's net-versus-par measure at −4.

The third day was the opposite extreme: +12 net of par, +27 gross, the worst round of Mullin's career to date. It made no difference whatsoever. Henry Meller, who at one stage trailed by 30, pulled 12 shots back over the closing stretch and still finished 18 adrift. Baker's recovery was smaller in scale: 19 behind at his lowest point, closed to 12 by the end of the final round at Palmares, the first visit to the Robert Trent Jones Jr. course. Neither got close enough to make the last day matter.

title: Thirty-Four Pars and a Hatful of Nines

articles.headline: Jon Baker's Pars Break The Field
articles.standfirst: Six points clear of Gregg Williams over four Kent links, the champion never finished a round worse than third of five — and his 44 at Littlestone was where the argument ended.
paragraphs: Jon Baker took the lead in the TEG 13 Trophy at the second hole of the opening round at Royal Cinque Ports and then, with one brief lapse in security, refused to give it back. He finished on 158 points, six clear of Gregg Williams.

The lapse came late on the second day. Baker had held the Stableford lead for 32 holes across two rounds when a par at the 16th at Prince's Dunes/Himalayas proved insufficient, and Gregg Williams moved in front. Baker had it back almost immediately. Williams's tenure at the summit was real, was earned, and is best measured in minutes.

Round three at Littlestone, the third of four links courses in Kent, was where the matter was settled. From the 8th to the 11th he did not drop a gross shot: par, birdie at the short 9th, par at the stroke-index-one 10th, par. Thirteen points across four holes. It has the rhythm of a man filing paperwork correctly. His gross round of 79, eight over par, is the second-best gross round recorded in TEG history to that point. Gregg Williams, to his considerable credit, answered with 15 points from the 6th to the 10th and his own best gross of the tournament, 86, and the pair finished the day level at the top of the Trophy, with Baker also leading the TEG 13 Green Jacket.
Across the four rounds Baker recorded 34 pars or better, an all-time TEG record.

articles.headline: Forty-Nine At Littlestone, Eights Everywhere Else
articles.standfirst: John Patterson arrived as the TEG 12 Trophy holder, posted the third-best round in TEG history and a personal-best gross at Littlestone, and bracketed it with quadruple bogeys at Royal Cinque Ports and Prince's — finishing six points clear of the Spoon.
paragraphs: John Patterson's TEG 13 was a study in extremes across four Kent links, all four of them new to him.

It began badly. At Royal Cinque Ports he opened with an 8 at the 1st, added a 9 at the 7th, another 8 at the 10th and a 9 at the par-5 16th, the last of which deposited him at the bottom of the TEG 13 Wooden Spoon race. He signed for 108. Friday at Prince's Dunes/Himalayas offered no revision of the thesis: 11 shots bled over the first four holes, another eight lost between the 13th and 15th, 8s at the 1st and the 17th, 105 on the card and 28 points.

Then Littlestone. Patterson went round in 83, a personal-best gross round at +12, and took 49 Stableford points, the third-best round in TEG history to date. He gathered 13 points in four holes from the 8th, including a net eagle at the stroke-index-one 10th, and still found room for a 7 at the par-3 17th. The 21-point swing between the Friday round and the Saturday was the swing of the tournament.

The final round at Prince's Shore/Dunes settled at 36 points, 13 fewer. It contained both his best and worst single holes of the tournament: an eagle three at the par-5 2nd, the only eagle recorded by anyone in TEG 13 and the first eagle in TEG history, and a 9 at the par-5 15th. He is the only man ever to have made an eagle in this competition. He is also, on the same scorecard, entirely capable of a nine.

articles.headline: David Mullin Completes The Spoon Hat-Trick
articles.standfirst: Eight prior Green Jackets, two prior Trophies and the most consistent scoring of anyone here still added up to 135 points and last place, sealed by a nine at Prince's tenth.
paragraphs: David Mullin finished in Kent with 135 Stableford points, the lowest total in the field, and collected the TEG 13 Wooden Spoon. It is his third in succession.

Nothing about it was sudden. Across four links courses, none of which he had played before in TEG competition, his gross scores were 94 at Royal Cinque Ports, 89 over Prince's Dunes/Himalayas, 92 at Littlestone and 92 on the Shore/Dunes combination that closed the tournament. Five strokes separate his best round from his worst. In most walks of life that reliability would be a virtue. Here it functioned as a tether, keeping him within reach of the bottom place from Thursday onwards.

The matter was formalised at the 10th at Prince's in the final round. Mullin took nine shots on the par 4. A quintuple bogey, no Stableford points, on a stroke index 3 hole. It is the worst score he has recorded on a par 4 in TEG competition, which given the sample size available is a genuine achievement of sorts. He arrived at the tee fourth from bottom in the Spoon race. He left it last. He stayed there.

The Spoon is decided on Stableford points, and 135 across four rounds was never going to be enough to escape it. Mullin's tournament was defined less by disaster than by the complete absence of any round good enough to lift him clear.

articles.headline: Alex Baker Saves His Best For Last
articles.standfirst: Last in the Wooden Spoon race at Littlestone's ninth after an eight at the second, Alex Baker replied at Prince's with 44 points and the best gross round of his TEG career.
paragraphs: Alex Baker's time in Kent turned on its final two days. Littlestone, on the Saturday, was where it came apart. He opened with a double bogey, then a quadruple-bogey eight at the 2nd and another double at the 3rd. Eight gross shots gone in three holes, and the round barely under way. The bleeding resumed at the turn: a triple bogey at the 8th, a double at the par-three 9th and another double at the 10th cost seven more. The five at the 9th was the decisive one. It dropped him to the bottom of the TEG 13 Wooden Spoon race, last of the five, having begun the hole a place clear. He signed for 32 points and a gross 100.

It was not an isolated event so much as a habit. He had run up a quadruple-bogey eight at the 11th at Royal Cinque Ports in round one, going three holes from the 10th without a net par, and at Prince's on the Friday he closed with five consecutive double bogeys, ten shots dropped over the last five holes. There is something almost administrative about five straight doubles. Nothing worsened. Nothing improved. The hours simply passed.

The answer came on the Sunday at Prince's Shore/Dunes. Baker made pars at the 1st and 2nd, then paired them again at the 9th and 10th, and came home in +17 gross, a personal best for a single round. His 44 points were a 12-point improvement on Littlestone.

articles.headline: Eighteen Clear: Jon Baker's Third Straight Jacket
articles.standfirst: The gross lead was nine after Royal Cinque Ports and only ever grew; a +8 at Littlestone, the second-best gross round TEG has recorded, turned a competition into an inspection.
paragraphs: Jon Baker won the TEG 13 Green Jacket with a gross total of +50, finishing eighteen shots clear of Gregg Williams. It is the lowest gross aggregate recorded in TEG history, and comfortably the best of Baker's own career.

The margin was built on consistency across four links courses, all of them new to the field on this first visit to Kent. Baker opened with 85 at Royal Cinque Ports, added 88 over Prince's Dunes/Himalayas, and closed with 85 on the Shore/Dunes combination. Fifty over par for four rounds is not golf anyone would frame. It was, in this field, an act of near-monastic discipline. The round that separated him came on the Saturday at Littlestone, where he went round in 79, eight over par and the second-best gross round anyone has produced in a TEG. By the end of that third day he led the Jacket outright, and he also headed the TEG 13 Trophy on Stableford, level at the top with nothing between him and the chasing player.

The underlying number explains the eighteen shots. Baker made 34 pars or better across the four rounds, more than any player has managed in a single TEG. That is an average of better than eight clean holes a round on unfamiliar links. Against the rest of this scorecard evidence, it borders on the discourteous, and it left his rivals with no route back into the gross contest at any stage.

title: Nine Ahead, Two Home: Mullin's Kent Double

articles.headline: Mullin Survives the Sixteenth
articles.standfirst: A three-time Wooden Spoon holder turned Trophy champion held off a grandstand finish from Alex Baker, whose charge was undone by the same nightmare hole that had wrecked his tournament three rounds earlier.
paragraphs: David Mullin won the Trophy with 154 points, two clear of Alex Baker. It is the 16th-best total in TEG history and the third-best of his own career, and very nearly all of it was banked before anyone thought to object.

The foundation was laid on the first two links. At Royal Cinque Ports he went round in 87, seven strokes better than his previous visit. The engine room was a four-hole run from the 9th: par, birdie at the 10th, then two more pars, 13 points, a man briefly playing golf on purpose. The sequence ended at the 13th with a double bogey. At Littlestone he shot 85, again seven better than last time out, and another course best.

Prince's declined to co-operate. In round three he arrived at the par-five 8th with a tournament in his pocket and took nine. A quadruple bogey. It returned nothing, which is the standard yield on a nine. He then took 13 points from the closing four holes, three pars and a birdie at the last, as though the 8th had happened to a stranger. Round four produced another quadruple bogey, an eight at the 10th. Two quads on the same links in two days. The trophy did not appear to mind.

That opened the door for Baker, who had trailed by as many as nine. He answered with 10 points across the first three holes of the final round and 11 more from the 13th to the 15th, closing to within two. Then he reached the 16th and made a ten. His four days had begun to come apart considerably earlier, at Littlestone, where he dropped 12 shots across holes 2 to 5.

articles.headline: The Sixteenth Strikes Twice
articles.standfirst: Two different courses, the same hole number, and the same catastrophic 10 — bookending a tournament Alex Baker otherwise nearly won.
paragraphs: Two of Baker's four rounds in Kent ended with a 10 on the card, and on both occasions the number arrived at a hole numbered 16. Different courses, different pars, no connection whatsoever beyond the obvious one. The first came in the opening round at Royal Cinque Ports, a quintuple bogey at the par-five 16th, stroke index 7, no Stableford points. The second, at Prince's on the Sunday, was worse in relative terms: a 10 at a par four, a sextuple bogey, on stroke index 17, the second-easiest hole on the card. Taking ten shots there requires a degree of commitment.

The Prince's 10 was the more painful for what preceded it. Baker had played the 13th, 14th and 15th in par, par, par, three holes without dropping a gross shot, worth eleven Stableford points. The 16th erased the lot at a stroke. He was not alone in losing his footing there. Jon Baker arrived at the same hole having gone par-birdie-birdie-par-par from the 11th, and made a double bogey for no points.

These were the headline numbers, not the only ones. Baker also had an 8 at the 11th at Royal Cinque Ports, a 9 at the 5th and an 8 at the 8th at Littlestone, and an 8 at the 10th at Prince's in round three. Five further holes returning nothing. His round-one 98 at Royal Cinque Ports was still four strokes better than his previous visit, which tells you a good deal about the previous visit.

articles.headline: Twelve Down to Seven, Never in Doubt
articles.standfirst: David Mullin's gross lead shrank by five shots in the final round alone, but the Green Jacket was never seriously threatened.
paragraphs: David Mullin took the Green Jacket at TEG 14 with a gross total of +68, seven clear of Jon Baker. His ninth. It is the sixth-best Green Jacket total on record and the fourth-best of his own career at the metric.

The number was built on consistency across Kent's four links rounds. Mullin set a personal best on every course he played: 87 at Royal Cinque Ports and 85 at Littlestone, each seven strokes better than his previous visit in TEG 13, and 91 at Prince's Shore/Dunes, one better than before. None of those figures would trouble a club noticeboard in isolation. Stacked together, they were unanswerable.

Behind him the chase was real, and late. Baker trailed by 15 at one point and closed to seven, the bulk of that work arriving in the final round at Prince's, where his 83 gross set a new course record. The previous mark of 85 had stood across five prior visits, and was Baker's own. Gregg Williams made up more ground still, trailing by 18 at his worst and finishing eight back. His +76 is a personal-best Green Jacket gross total, and his 86 at Prince's in round three was a course best for him too.
The gap never closed far enough. Mullin's margin of seven at the finish flatters the field, given how much larger it had been for most of the four days.

articles.headline: Twelve Shots Adrift, No Argument
articles.standfirst: Jon Baker was worst in the field in two separate rounds, and the final one came a day too late to change anything.
paragraphs: Jon Baker finished last in the Stableford count and took the Wooden Spoon with 125 points across the four rounds. The defence of a title can take many forms. He chose this one, and won it by 12, which is a margin of some authority.

The early links did him no favours, and he returned the courtesy. At Royal Cinque Ports his best gross was 92, seven strokes worse than the 85 he had managed on his previous visit. At Littlestone he posted 92 against a prior best of 79. Thirteen shots is not a bad day; it is a change of identity. His third round at Prince's brought 28 points, held down in part by a run of pars from the 14th that ended with a triple bogey six at the par-three 17th.

The final round was another man entirely. Baker returned 39 points, an improvement of 11 on the previous day, and his 83 gross set a new course record for Prince's Shore/Dunes, beating the previous mark of 85 that had stood across five prior visits. It was also his personal best on the layout, two strokes better than his last time there. The scoring came in a burst: five holes without dropping a gross shot from the 11th to the 15th, back-to-back birdies at the 12th and 13th, a two-hole birdie streak that equals the all-time TEG record, and 14 points across holes 12 to 15.

Then the 16th, which had already relieved Alex Baker of the Trophy that afternoon, took a double bogey from Jon and ended the run. He ran up an eight at the 18th. He therefore holds the course record and the Wooden Spoon at the same time, which takes some arranging.

articles.headline: Williams's Best Week, Nobody Noticed
articles.standfirst: An 18-shot deficit after a blown-up third hole didn't stop Gregg Williams closing hard and posting his best-ever TEG gross total.
paragraphs: Williams finished TEG 14 with a Gross total of +76, a personal best, and no prize of any description. The number rested on two course records of his own: 93 at Royal Cinque Ports, one better than his previous mark there of 94, and 86 at Prince's in round three, three strokes better than his last visit and inside his previous best of 89.

It was not tidy. He opened at Deal with a 9 at the par-five 3rd, stroke index 4, a quadruple bogey worth nothing at all. Littlestone was worse in the wider sense: 97, eleven strokes adrift of the 86 he had managed there before, and only 27 Stableford points.

Round three was the correction. He gained twelve points on the day, reaching 39, and the middle of it was genuinely solid: pars at the 9th, 10th and 11th for nine points, three holes without dropping a gross shot, then two more clean holes at the 15th and 16th. Between those came an 8 at the par-five 12th, which brought the exhibition to a close.

Sunday offered more steadiness in patches, gross pars at the 5th and 6th and again at the 14th and 15th. Having trailed the Green Jacket lead by 18 at one stage, he closed to within 8. Ten shots recovered. Eight still owed.

articles.headline: Williams Banks the Trophy in Sintra
articles.standfirst: Gregg Williams led the TEG 15 Trophy from the fourth hole of the opening round at Estoril, won three of the four rounds outright, and had the thing settled long before Oitavos Dunes.
paragraphs: Gregg Williams won the TEG 15 Trophy on 157 points, finishing 21 clear of runner-up Stuart Neumann across the four rounds on the Lisbon Coast. He took the lead at the fourth hole of Round 1 and was never afterwards asked to hand it back.

The defining round of the trip came on the Monday at Penha Longa, the Atlantic course at Sintra, where Williams signed for 82 gross. That is a Penha Longa course record. The previous mark of 86 had stood through six prior visits and was presumed safe. It was also a personal best gross round for Williams at +10, and it removed 14 strokes from the 96 he had posted on his only previous visit to the course. He won three rounds outright. Nobody stopped him, though several appeared to be trying to draw attention away from themselves.

The rest was steady rather than spectacular by that standard. He opened with 86 at Estoril, a course new to the field, and closed with 91 at Oitavos Dunes, two strokes better than the 93 he managed there in TEG 8 and a course best for him.

The one clear blemish came in Round 2 at West Cliffs. Williams arrived at the par-five 15th and left it with a 10. The quintuple bogey returned no Stableford points at all, which is a rare thing to achieve while still holding the tournament in your hand. It left him with 88 for the round. Given the eventual margin, it cost him nothing but the scorecard. By the time he reached Oitavos Dunes on the Tuesday, the Trophy had stopped being a contest and become an appointment.

articles.headline: The Spoon Stays in the Family
articles.standfirst: Alex Baker takes the Wooden Spoon straight from his brother Jon Baker on 114 points, 11 adrift of anyone else, after making an 11 and two 10s across Rounds 2 and 3.
paragraphs: Alex Baker finished on 114 points and collected the TEG 15 Wooden Spoon, taking it directly from his brother Jon, the holder, which at least keeps the item in the family. The damage was concentrated rather than spread. Two rounds, and inside those rounds two short stretches, did nearly all of the work.

The first came at West Cliffs in round two, on a links course none of the field had played before. At the 6th, a par 5, Alex Baker signed for an 11: a sextuple bogey, and the worst he has recorded on a par 5. He followed it with a 9 at the 7th and a 7 at the 8th. Thirteen shots dropped in three holes, and not a net par to show for any of it. Later the same afternoon he took 10 at the 17th. The round came to 110 gross, which under the circumstances counts as containment.

Penha Longa the next day produced the same shape in a different setting. Nine at the 12th, six at the 13th and 10 at the 14th cost him 12 shots across three holes, again with no net par among them. He still signed for 106, matching precisely the gross he made here on his previous visit in TEG 8. Consistency of a sort.

The closing round offered something better. His 103 at Oitavos Dunes was a shot inside the 104 he posted there in TEG 8, a course best, arriving one round too late to trouble the standings or the destination of the Spoon.

articles.headline: Mullin Eagles, Then Falls Apart at Oitavos
articles.standfirst: David Mullin came to Portugal holding both TEG 14 titles, made the only eagle anyone managed, and finished with the worst round and worst gross round of his TEG career.
paragraphs: David Mullin produced the single most eye-catching swing of TEG 15 and also its most punishing collapse. He is a man of nine Green Jackets and the defending Trophy champion, and he conducted both halves of this with the same unruffled bearing.

The high point came at West Cliffs in round two, where he holed out for a three at the par-5 15th. It was the only eagle struck by anyone in the tournament. The same round contained a 10 at the par-5 6th, a quintuple bogey worth nothing whatsoever, and by the 11th, a triple bogey at another blank hole, Mullin had slipped from fourth to last in the TEG 15 Wooden Spoon race.

Round three at Penha Longa opened as well as any stretch of his four days: par, birdie, par for 10 points through three holes. Then a triple bogey at the 4th, the hardest hole on the card, closed the account. He still signed for 85 gross there, one stroke better than his previous best at the course.

Oitavos Dunes undid all of it. Mullin began with a quadruple-bogey 8 at the 1st and finished with another 8 at the 18th, closing with four consecutive holes without a net par. The round came in at 22 points and +33 gross, both the worst figures of his TEG career to date. His 104 at Oitavos was 16 strokes worse than the 88 he had managed on his only previous visit. He remains the defending champion, which is a fact, and this remains the worst round he has ever played, which is also a fact.

articles.headline: Neumann Turns 115 Into Second Place
articles.standfirst: Stuart Neumann's West Cliffs round contained an 11, two 9s and a 10, and he still finished second in the Trophy — better than any of his last four TEGs.
paragraphs: Stuart Neumann's TEG 15 was built on holes that got away from him. It began at Estoril, where a 9 at the par-four 3rd was followed by a 10 at the par-four 15th. Six over on a single hole, and the worst he has recorded on a par four. He signed for 106 on a course none of the field had played before.

Round 2 at West Cliffs, another first visit, was worse. Stuart made an 8 at the 4th, a 10 at the par-five 6th, an 11 at the par-five 13th, a 9 at the 14th and a 9 at the 17th. Five holes, 26 shots over par between them, not one of them returning a point. The 9 at the 14th, the hardest hole on the card, dropped him to the bottom of the TEG 15 Wooden Spoon race. His gross total was 115. He kept playing. That should be noted.

Penha Longa turned it round. Stuart shot 92, seven strokes better than his 99 there in TEG 8 and a course best, with three straight pars-or-better against his handicap at the 14th, 15th and 16th worth nine points.

The pattern had not gone away, though. At Oitavos Dunes he closed with a 9 at the 18th, part of a 99 that left him four shots off the 95 he managed there in TEG 8. A man can drop 26 shots across five holes and still finish second in the Trophy. That is not a remark about Neumann. It is a remark about everybody else.

articles.headline: Williams's First Jacket, Won By Twenty-Nine
articles.standfirst: Gregg Williams had never won a Green Jacket; he won all four rounds of this one and finished 29 clear of Jon Baker at +63.
paragraphs: Gregg Williams had never won a Green Jacket. He now has one, and he acquired it in a manner that discourages debate: a gross total of +63, the TEG 15 Green Jacket by 29 strokes from Jon Baker, and every single round of the gross won. It is the best gross total of his career.

The third round at Penha Longa settled it. Williams went round in 82 gross, +10, a new course record, beating the previous mark of 86 established across six prior visits. It stands as the best gross round of his career. It was also a fourteen-stroke improvement on his own previous best at the mountain parkland course, the 96 he posted on his first visit there. He closed with 91 at Oitavos Dunes, two better than his previous best there. The 82 had already made the closing round decorative.

Baker was the nearest challenger and had genuine moments, including an 85 at Penha Longa, six strokes better than his previous best on the course, and a 94 at Oitavos Dunes. The trouble had been arranged a day earlier at West Cliffs, where he ran up an 11 at the par-four 17th. A septuple bogey, and the worst score he has recorded on a par four. Against a leader in that form, one such hole is not a setback. It is a resignation.

articles.headline: Nineteen Points, Then a Ten
articles.standfirst: John Patterson gathered 19 points in six holes at Penha Longa, which only sharpened the contrast with a final round that opened with a sextuple-bogey 10 at the 1st.
paragraphs: For six holes on the Monday at Penha Longa, John Patterson played better than anyone else managed across the four days. From the 3rd to the 8th of round three he collected 19 Stableford points: pars at the 3rd, 5th, 6th and 7th, the last of those a four-pointer on the stroke index 4 short hole, and bogeys at the 4th and 8th that still banked three apiece.

The course then asked for it back, with interest. The 9th, 10th and 11th cost him eight shots against par, including a quadruple-bogey 8 at the 10th, and the stroke index 1 16th took a quintuple-bogey 9. He signed for a 99, his best gross of the tournament, on a course he was seeing for the first time.

Tuesday at Oitavos Dunes began worse. Patterson took 10 on the opening par 4, a sextuple bogey, then added double bogeys at the 2nd and the 3rd. Ten shots gone in three holes, no net par among them, and the round barely under way. The middle stretch was the same story told again: doubles at the 9th, 10th, 11th and 13th around a quadruple-bogey 7 at the par-3 12th, twelve shots dropped across five holes. A quadruple-bogey 8 at the 17th completed the paperwork. His 105 was his highest round of the tournament, and his four blow-up holes there accounted for 16 shots on their own.

articles.headline: Two Spoons Later, the Trophy's His
articles.standfirst: Stuart Neumann led the Trophy from the fourth hole of the tournament and was never seriously troubled again, closing out a first career win by 13 points.
paragraphs: Stuart Neumann won the Trophy at TEG 16 on the Lisbon Coast with 156 Stableford points, finishing 13 clear of Gregg Williams. It is the 16th-highest Trophy total recorded and the second-best of his own career. A man can wait a long time for a first Trophy. Neumann waited, and then won it by rather more than he needed to.

The margin was built early and never surrendered. He held the Trophy lead after round two at Troia, still held it after round three at Penha Longa, and carried it through the closing round at Estoril. Williams, meanwhile, led the Jacket standings at each of those same checkpoints. For three days the two of them occupied separate thrones, and neither gave an inch in his own.

The final round was not flawless. At Estoril's 8th, a par 4 and the hardest hole on the card at stroke index 1, Neumann took nine. A quintuple bogey. Worth no points at all, which is to say the hole may as well not have happened, and in scoring terms it did not. The lead never so much as shifted in its seat. That is what a cushion is for.

Estoril otherwise gave him his best golf of the four days. His 92 there was a course personal best, 14 strokes better than the 106 he posted on his only previous visit in TEG 15. It was the one venue of the four where he improved on his own history, and he chose the day the Trophy was settled to do it.

articles.headline: The 12th at Penha Longa Claims Both Bakers & Baker Breaks Two Records — Both the Wrong Way
articles.standfirst: Jon and Alex Baker, brothers in the same field, both came unstuck at the same par-5 in Round 3 — one with a quintuple bogey, the other a quadruple. Alex Baker propped up the Trophy table from the first hole of the tournament and closed it out by setting new course-worst marks at both ends of the week.
paragraphs: Alex Baker's tournament began badly and then declined to change course. In the first round at Oitavos Dunes he took nine at the 1st, nine at the 11th and ten at the 17th, signing for 113 gross. That is a new course-worst for Oitavos, beating the previous mark of 111 set across twelve prior visits. Twelve visits' worth of human frailty, surpassed before lunch on day one. At Troia the next day the damage was more concentrated: thirteen shots dropped over the five holes from the 13th to the 17th, three triples followed by two doubles.

Round three took the field to Penha Longa, where both Bakers found the same piece of ground. Jon Baker made a double bogey six at the 11th, then took ten at the par-five 12th, a quintuple bogey and no points, and followed it with an eight at the 13th. Eleven shots gone in three holes, three holes without a net par. It was his only round of the tournament in which he failed to improve on a previous visit: 97 gross at a course where his prior best was 85.

Alex was on the same holes, doing much the same thing at a marginally gentler gradient. Double bogey at the 11th, then a nine at the 12th for quadruple bogey, then a seven at the 13th and a seven at the 14th. Twelve shots dropped across four holes and, like his brother, three holes from the 12th onward without a net par. Whatever the 12th at Penha Longa is, it is in the family.

The final round at Estoril separated them. Jon's one lapse came at the 11th, the hardest hole on the card, where he made an eight, and that was the extent of it. Alex's round was a lapse with holes attached. Nine at the 1st. Eight at the 3rd. Nine at the 6th. Fourteen shots bled over the six holes from the 5th to the 10th, every single one a double or worse, an unbroken run of ruin conducted with no apparent loss of composure. Then the 12th, a par four, where he took eleven. A septuple bogey, and the worst score he has ever recorded on a par four in his life. The round came to 107 gross, a second course-worst of the four days, exceeding Estoril's previous high of 106 across six prior visits. He finished on 127 points and collected the Wooden Spoon, his third, and the second in a row. He did not merely lose. He amended the record books at two separate venues while doing it.

articles.headline: A Course Record, One Day After the Wheels Came Off
articles.standfirst: David Mullin shot the worst round of his tournament at Penha Longa, then came back the next day to break the Estoril course record.
paragraphs: David Mullin's tournament ended a very long way from where it started. At Oitavos Dunes in the opening round he ran up a triple-bogey seven at the 10th, a stroke index 4 par four, and the zero points dropped him from second to fifth in the Wooden Spoon race. Fifth in the Spoon race is not a mid-table sort of fifth. It is the bottom of the pile. Round three at Penha Longa was worse in places: a quadruple-bogey eight at the 16th, the hardest hole on the card, after which he composed himself and parred 17 and 18 like a man tidying a room he had just set fire to. The round came to 30 points, and his 98 there was well adrift of his previous best at the course.

Estoril, on the Tuesday, was a different matter. Mullin birdied the 2nd and parred the 3rd, then wobbled through a bogey-bogey-double stretch at the 4th, 5th and 6th before a birdie at the 7th stopped the slide. The back nine simply held. Nine points from the 11th, 12th and 13th, with pars at 12 and 13, and two more pars at 16 and 17 to finish.

The total was 45 points, a 15-point improvement on round three. The gross number mattered more. His 80 set a new course record at Estoril, beating the previous mark of 86 established across six prior visits, and bettered his own best there, a 94 at TEG 15, by fourteen strokes. Four days earlier he had been last in the race for the Spoon. Golf is not a fair sport, but it is occasionally a generous one.

articles.headline: Best in the Field, Every Time
articles.standfirst: Gregg Williams topped the gross leaderboard in every round of the tournament, seeing off a grandstand finish from David Mullin, who broke the Estoril course record along the way.
paragraphs: Gregg Williams's second Green Jacket was never really in doubt, and the final margin, 16 shots clear of David Mullin, says as much. His gross total of +66 is the fifth-best in the event's history and comfortably the best of his own career. It was, by any measure, thoroughly deserved.

It was also not tidy. Troia, a course none of the field had seen before, produced a 94 and two of his worst passages of the tournament: four holes from the 8th without a net par, then three straight doubles from the 13th, six gross shots gone in as many holes.

Penha Longa on the Monday was similarly uneven. A triple at the 3rd and a double at the 4th were answered at once with a birdie at the short 5th, a repair immediately undone by a bogey-triple-double run through the 6th, 7th and 8th. He then steadied himself, playing the 11th through the 15th in level par and collecting nine points across the last three of those. His 87 was five worse than his previous visit here.

Estoril produced both his best round and his loudest mistake. The 80 was a course best by six on his only prior visit, and it arrived despite an eight at the par-four 14th, a quadruple bogey, and a double at the 9th that ended a run of three straight pars. He won the Jacket by 16. He did not avoid the wreckage. He was simply the man whose wreckage cost him least.

articles.headline: Fourth Place, No More
articles.standfirst: After three straight TEGs stuck in fourth, Jon Baker builds an 18-point Trophy win the hard way — round after round, never worse than second.
paragraphs: Jon Baker won the TEG 17 Trophy with 166 Stableford points, 18 clear of runner-up David Mullin. It is the highest Trophy total of his career. Three years of fourth place had begun to look less like a run of results and more like a permanent seating arrangement. He has now vacated the chair.

The shape of the win was steady rather than sudden. After two rounds Baker sat on top of the Stableford table, though only level at the front, with Mullin leading the TEG 17 Green Jacket on gross. Baker's second round at West Cliffs was an 86, fifteen strokes better than the 101 he had posted on his only previous visit to the Cynthia Dye links. Fifteen strokes is a great deal of improvement. It also implies a great deal of 101.

Round three at Royal Óbidos settled it. Baker went round Seve Ballesteros's parkland course in 86 gross, a new course record. The previous best was 87, set across 18 prior visits by the group. Eighteen visits, and the bar had been left at a height a grown man could step over without breaking stride. Baker stepped over it. It was also a personal best there by three shots, and eight better than his last time out on the course.

The final round back at Praia D'El Rey produced one more entry in the record books. Baker birdied the fourth and fifth holes back to back, a two-hole birdie streak that equals the all-time TEG record. The all-time record for consecutive birdies in TEG is two. It has stood for some years, presumably out of a shared sense of realism.

He finished on 92 gross at Praia D'El Rey in that closing round, matching his score from the previous visit rather than bettering it, the act of a man conserving himself for the presentation. By then the margin was long since established. Mullin, whose own 82 at West Cliffs was a course personal best, could not close the gap.

articles.headline: Leader, Loser, Fighter, Fallen
articles.standfirst: Patterson topped the Trophy table after Round 1, then produced the tournament's worst gross round, fought back in Round 3, and blew up again in Round 4.
paragraphs: John Patterson's four days ran to extremes. He opened with a 96 at Praia D'El Rey, good enough to lead the Trophy race, then went to West Cliffs and signed for 116: a gross round of +44, the worst of his career to date, and 19 strokes more than he had taken on his only previous visit to the links.

The damage was concentrated in one stretch. Between the 8th and the 15th he dropped 27 shots in eight holes: a double, three triple bogeys, another double, a 10 at the par-five 13th and an 11 at the par-five 15th. That 11, six over par, is the worst score relative to par he has recorded on any hole in TEG. He had to travel a long way into the round to find it, and he found it. The triple bogey at the 10th dropped him to the bottom of the TEG 17 Wooden Spoon race.

Royal Óbidos brought the correction, and it was a proper one. Patterson went from 22 points in Round 2 to 41 in Round 3, a swing of 19, and his 94 was a course personal best, seven strokes better than his previous visit there. For one afternoon he looked like a man who had solved something.

The recovery did not hold. Back at Praia D'El Rey for the final round, he ran up a 10 at the par-four 15th, the stroke index three hole, another six-over sextuple bogey and another blank on the card, undoing much of what Round 3 had rebuilt.

articles.headline: The Baker Who Couldn't Stop Bleeding Shots
articles.standfirst: From a course-worst 114 at Praia D'El Rey to a 25-shot horror stretch in the final round, Alex Baker's week reads as one long cautionary tale.
paragraphs: Alex Baker found something to lose in all four rounds of TEG 17 on the Lisbon Coast, and the worst of it came first. His opening 114 at Praia D'El Rey is the highest gross round ever recorded at the course, beating the previous worst of 110 set across 24 prior visits. The centrepiece was a 10 at the par-4 5th, stroke index 2, a sextuple bogey inside the first hour. He had made his position clear while the field was still applying sunscreen.

Round two at West Cliffs was quieter but still leaky: ten shots gone across holes 9 to 11, with quadruple bogeys at the 10th and 11th, then eight more over 13 to 15. It was, oddly, his best round of the tournament in relative terms. His 105 there is a personal best at West Cliffs, five shots better than his only previous visit, which says rather more about the other three rounds than it does about the 105.

Royal Óbidos produced another 10, this time at the par-4 14th in round three. Then came the return to Praia D'El Rey, where Baker bled 25 shots between the 5th and the 13th, a nine-hole run without a single hole played in better than double bogey. Nine holes. Not one of them recoverable. Quadruple bogeys at the par-5 12th and the 13th ended a three-hole stretch without a net par.

His 111 in that final round was the best of his four scores, but still eleven shots adrift of his last visit here and eleven off his course best of 100, set at TEG 9. The bucket was smaller by then. It was still a bucket with a hole in it.

articles.headline: From the Podium to the Cellar
articles.standfirst: The back-to-back Jacket champion never left the bottom half all tournament, and a horror stretch at Royal Óbidos sealed the Wooden Spoon.
paragraphs: Gregg Williams, the back-to-back Jacket champion, a man with four Trophy wins already in the cabinet, finished TEG 17 on 123 Stableford points. That was enough to hand him the TEG 17 Wooden Spoon.

The damage was concentrated. The clearest single stretch came on the back nine at Royal Óbidos in round three, where Williams played the closing seven holes, the 12th through the 18th, without a net par. Every one of the seven was a double bogey: a 6 at the par-four 12th, a 5 at the short 13th, 6s at the 14th, 16th and 17th, a 5 at the par-three 15th and a 7 at the par-five 18th. Seven holes, seven doubles, no deviation whatsoever. There is a certain dignity in a man who finds his level and then refuses, on principle, to leave it. The run yielded six points where par figures would have produced fourteen, a shortfall of eight.
Royal Óbidos has not been a happy course for him. This was his fourth visit, and his best gross there on this trip, 99, was two strokes worse than his previous trip and two off his course best of 97.

The final round at Praia D'El Rey opened badly too, Williams running up a 9 at the first, a quintuple bogey that returned nothing. As opening statements go, it required no elaboration. The one bright note was elsewhere on the same course: his 93 in round one was seven strokes better than his last visit, and matched his best gross at Praia D'El Rey.

articles.headline: West Cliffs Breaks Both Ways
articles.standfirst: In Round 2 at West Cliffs, David Mullin carded the new course record while John Patterson set the course-worst — on the very same day.
paragraphs: The second round of TEG 17 took the field to West Cliffs, the Cynthia Dye links at Óbidos, on Sunday 6 October, only the second time the course had been used. It produced both ends of the register in a single afternoon.

David Mullin shot 82 gross, a new West Cliffs course record. The previous mark was 88. It was also comfortably his own best at the course: he had gone round in 94 on his only previous visit, in TEG 15, so this was twelve strokes better.

John Patterson went the other way, and went thoroughly. His 116 gross set a new course worst, one shot beyond the previous high of 115, and at +44 it was the worst gross round of his career. He had shot 97 here in TEG 15, making this visit nineteen strokes heavier.

The damage was concentrated. Between the 8th and the 15th Patterson dropped 27 shots in eight holes: a double bogey at the 8th, then triple bogeys at the 9th, 10th and 11th, a double at the short 12th, a ten at the par-five 13th, a triple at the 14th and an eleven at the par-five 15th. Six of those eight holes returned no Stableford points at all. The card, at that point, was less a record of golf than a witness statement.
Same course, same day, 34 shots between them.

articles.headline: One Hole in the Sun
articles.standfirst: David Mullin held the Green Jacket lead for exactly one hole in Round 3 before Jon Baker took it straight back and never let go.
paragraphs: Jon Baker won the TEG 17 Green Jacket at +67 gross, 13 clear of David Mullin. It is the third-best gross total of Baker's career.

The margin conceals how long the outcome stayed open. Baker took the lead at the second hole of Round 1 at Praia D'El Rey and held it for 35 holes across three rounds, only to hand it over at the very first hole of Round 3 at Royal Óbidos, where he took six on the par-four opening hole for a double bogey and a single Stableford point. Thirty-five holes of authority, surrendered before anyone had settled. Mullin was the beneficiary, and he had earned the position: his 82 gross at West Cliffs in Round 2 is a new course record there, beating the previous mark of 88 set across six prior visits, and it was a 12-stroke improvement on his own score at the course a TEG earlier.

Baker did not stay behind for long. He recovered the lead and then extended it, and the last two rounds became a procession rather than a contest. His scoring at the two links-influenced venues supported it: 86 at West Cliffs, 15 strokes better than his previous visit and a course personal best, and 86 at Royal Óbidos, also a course best, three better than his previous mark there. Mullin held the Jacket for a single hole and finished 13 back. A tenure best measured in yards.

articles.headline: Baker Wins It on Day One
articles.standfirst: A 46 in the opening round put twelve points between Alex Baker and John Patterson; across the next three days the runner-up took back only four of them.
paragraphs: Alex Baker won the Trophy at TEG 18 in Catalonia with 169 Stableford points, eight clear of runner-up John Patterson. It is the seventh-highest total on record and the second best of his own career. A man who already owns three Wooden Spoons has now led a Trophy from the fifth hole of round one to the last. The record book has no way of registering surprise.

The points arrived in bursts, with long dry stretches in between. On the Tour Course in round one he took 17 from holes 8 to 12, three-point bogeys either side of pars at the 10th and 11th, then 13 more over holes 14 to 16, including a birdie at the par-5 15th. His 98 that day was his best gross of the four days on that course, though still six shots adrift of the 92 he had once posted there.

Round two was the same man, operated in reverse. He ran up an 11 at the par-5 18th and an eight at the par-3 16th, both blank holes, and signed for 106 gross. That is a new course-worst at PGA Catalunya Tour, one stroke worse than the 105 that had stood across 22 prior visits. Twenty-two visits of assembled human incompetence, and he surpassed the lot of them in an afternoon. He still led the Trophy at the end of the day.

He led after round three as well, propped up by 21 points across holes 11 to 16 on the Stadium Course. He led after round four too. He arrived at the 14th with the tournament in his pocket and took a 10 out of it. Then he added an eight at the 17th, in case anyone had missed the first gesture. The lead absorbed both without visible complaint.

articles.headline: Mullin Sets the Course Record, Loses the Jacket
articles.standfirst: An 11 at the 15th on Saturday, the lowest gross round the Stadium has ever given up on Monday, and nine shots gone in four holes on Tuesday.
paragraphs: David Mullin's trip to Catalonia swung between the best and the worst golf of the four days.

It began badly. On the 15th at the Tour Course in round one, a par 5 of stroke index 5, he ran up an eleven: a sextuple bogey, worth no Stableford points and the worst hole against par of his entire TEG career. Every hole he has ever played, and this one stands alone at the summit. It cost him ground in the Wooden Spoon race too, second in that competition before the hole and fifth after it.

Round three was the reverse. At the Stadium Course he shot 84 gross, the lowest round the course had ever surrendered, beating the previous record of 89 set across 27 prior visits. It was a personal best there as well. His best in five previous Stadium rounds was 91, and the 84 was eight shots better than his last visit. A course that had spent 27 visits refusing to yield anything under 89 handed him the lot in a single afternoon and asked for nothing in return.

Round four then unravelled over four holes. From the 14th to the 17th he went double bogey, triple bogey, double bogey, double bogey: 6, 8, 5, 6. Nine shots dropped in four holes, four holes without a net par, a single Stableford point on three of them and none at all at the 15th. The Stadium, having given away its record, spent the following day quietly reclaiming the interest.
He finished runner-up in the Green Jacket, 14 shots behind Gregg Williams, who won at +66.

articles.headline: Last Year's Double Winner Takes the Spoon
articles.standfirst: Jon Baker landed in Girona holding both the Trophy and the Green Jacket, led the gross for twenty holes, and finished 43 points behind his own brother.
paragraphs: Jon Baker arrived holding both titles and left holding the Wooden Spoon, his 126 Stableford points the total nobody wants. Twenty-three points adrift at the bottom, last in three rounds out of four. The handover was conducted with impressive efficiency.

It did not begin that way. He took the Green Jacket lead on the fifth hole of round one and held it for 20 holes, across into round two, before a bogey six at the par-five seventh on the Tour course handed the lead to Gregg Williams.

He answered on the same afternoon. Over the closing five holes he birdied the par-three 14th and parred 15, 16, 17 and 18, banking 16 points and covering the stretch one under par without dropping a gross shot anywhere in it. It put him back in front. After round two he led the Jacket, with Alex Baker top of the Trophy. This was the high-water mark, and he had two days left in which to demonstrate it.

Round three, on the Stadium course, undid the good work. He ran up a nine at the par-four fourth, a quintuple bogey worth no points at all. One hole, five over, nothing to show. Whatever remained of the defence was conducted from a considerable distance behind the front line.

The wider numbers tell the same story with less charity. This was his seventh visit to the Stadium course, and his best gross round there across the four days, 97, was eight strokes worse than the 89 he had once managed and eight worse than his last visit. On the Tour course, 87 against a previous best of 84. Seven visits to the Stadium have taught him a great deal about the Stadium. None of it appears to be usable.

articles.headline: Last After Four Holes, Second After Four Rounds
articles.standfirst: John Patterson dropped 22 shots between the 3rd and the 10th on the opening day, and still finished the closest thing Alex Baker had to a rival.
paragraphs: John Patterson's tournament was decided at both ends, and the first end came at speed. Four holes into round one on the Tour course he was already bottom of the Wooden Spoon race, down from fourth to fifth on the back of a quadruple-bogey eight at the 3rd and a triple-bogey seven at the 4th. The bleeding continued in an orderly fashion. He lost 22 shots to par across holes 3 to 10 and went seven straight holes, the 3rd to the 9th, without a net par.

Then he turned it around, which nobody had thought to ask him to do. Holes 13 to 16 brought him 13 points, and he finished round one 14 points stronger on the back nine than the front, for 34 points in all. Round two repeated the shape almost exactly: another quadruple-bogey eight, this time at the 4th, 11 shots dropped from the 6th to the 10th, then 16 points across holes 11 to 15. A man who has found a formula does not abandon it merely because the first half of it is a catastrophe.

The recovery held. In round four he took nine points from holes 4 to 6, and ended a run of bogeys or worse with a birdie at the 17th. Both courses yielded personal bests: 94 on the Tour, beating his previous 96, and 93 on the Stadium, beating his previous 95.
It was not enough. Alex Baker took the Trophy on 169 points, eight clear, with Patterson runner-up.

articles.headline: Williams Improves Every Round, Wins By Fourteen
articles.standfirst: Twenty-seven over par on Saturday and third of five; by Tuesday he had a personal-best 84 on the Stadium and the Green Jacket by a distance.
paragraphs: Gregg Williams started badly. On the Tour course he ran up a nine at the par-five 7th and an eight at the par-four 17th, both quadruple bogeys, and failed to make a par from the 2nd through the 14th before a birdie at the par-five 15th finally stopped the run. Thirteen holes without a par is not a slump so much as a policy. The round came to 31 points.

Round two was a different story: 42 points, eleven better. He took nine points from holes 3 to 5 and thirteen from 13 to 16, four consecutive pars without a gross shot dropped anywhere in them. The par at the 13th drew him level at the head of the Green Jacket, and during that same round Jon Baker's 20-hole spell in front ended with Williams overtaking him.

On the Stadium course a par at the 2nd put him outright in the lead. Four pars from the 2nd to the 5th were worth twelve points before a double bogey at the 6th closed the sequence. In round four he birdied the par-three 5th and gathered nine points from the 8th to the 10th, closing to nine off the Trophy lead having at one stage trailed by fifteen. His 84 that day was his best on the Stadium course, eight strokes better than his last visit there.

He finished on +66, fourteen clear of David Mullin: his own best gross total, and the sixth best ever recorded. The reigning Wooden Spoon holder has spent four days getting steadily better at golf, which is the sort of behaviour that ruins a reputation.
